title: The minimal surjective-strategy conjecture for wreath products
source: Peter Kagey, “Spinning switches on a wreath product”, arXiv:2210.09408 (2022). https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.09408
statement: Let $G\wr H$ be a wreath product with state group $K$, and call a surjective strategy **minimal** when it has the form $\{k_i\in K\}_{i=1}^{|K|-1}$. **Minimal strategy conjecture.** Whenever $G\wr H$ has a surjective strategy, it also has a minimal surjective strategy $\{k_i\in K\}_{i=1}^{|K|-1}$. Minimal strategies would give the shortest possible guaranteed bound discussed in the source; the conjecture is based on the examples known to the authors and remains open.
summary: For a generalized spinning-switches puzzle with switch group G, a finite set of positions on which the adversary's group H acts, and state group K = G^Ω: if a strategy (a fixed sequence of moves that reaches every state whatever the adversary does) exists, then one of the minimal possible length |K| - 1 exists. This is Conjecture 41 of Kagey. The proof classifies when a strategy exists at all: only when |K| = 1, when H acts trivially, or when G and the image of H are p-groups for the same prime p. The new part is the obstruction: an invariant on cosets of p-subgroups shows that a switch group that is not a p-group can never win, in cases the source's quotient argument does not reach (for example A_5). For p-groups a minimal strategy is built by induction through a central subgroup of order p fixed by H. Lean defines the puzzle through the actual semidirect product, includes the initial state, and proves by computation that a strategy exists in a small nontrivial case and does not exist for S_3.
paste_summary: Proved. If a generalized spinning-switches puzzle has a winning strategy, it has one of minimal length |K| - 1 (Kagey, arXiv:2210.09408, Conjecture 41). The proof classifies the puzzles with a strategy: |K| = 1, trivial action, or G and the image of H both p-groups for one prime.
